newsitem.title: FRANCE: Cr Lyonnais shares rise on recovery hopes.
newsitem.headline: Cr Lyonnais shares rise on recovery hopes.

text.p: Shares in French state-controlled bank Credit Lyonnais spurted higher on Monday on hopes it could be a turnaround story as the government sought to flesh out a privatisation plan for the bank promised for the end of March.
"It (Credit Lyonnais) seems to be the flavour of the month right now," said one analyst.
The non-voting shares in the bank, brought to the brink of collapse by a wild lending binge in the 1980s, closed up 5.05 percent at 204.50 francs on 135,236 shares traded.

Traders said the latest advance was triggered by an article in The Wall Street Journal quoting two investors suggesting the bank could replicate rebounds by some U.S. and Swedish banks and deliver rich returns for investors willing to jump in early.

The shares, which make up around 20 percent of its capital, have been rising steadily from a low of 94.55 francs last June. Last week, the shares got a boost when a newspaper reported the bank was on the verge of a strong profits recovery this year.
Some analysts said the bank's shares were undervalued and still had some distance to go. "We could see them to go to a minimum of 280 francs, possibly 310," said one Paris analyst.

But they were dismissive of talk it would be a spectacular turnaround story. "I have 230 francs as a 12-month horizon," said one analyst. "Even after it has got its act together, I'm not suggesting this will be a highly profitable bank," she said.
Meanwhile, the government buckled down to deliver its privatisation plan for the bank to the European Commission, which must approve new state aid by the end of March.

Analysts expect the plan to involve a capital injection of 12 billion francs to boost solvency ratios and offset capital losses on disposals demanded by Brussels in exchange for approving new state aid. It would be the third bailout plan for the bank in four years.

That sum would not include the cost of softening terms of a loan made by the bank under a 1995 state bailout to finance the spinoff of dud assets from its balance sheet estimated by the European Commission at 15 to 20 billion francs.
The plan, already late, had been promised for last week. But in a surprise last-minute decision on Friday, the government said it was postponing its submission.
One French newspaper said Brussels was not demanding major revisions to the plan but wanted more details about the cost.

Another newspaper said the government decided to delay the plan to give it time to figure out how it would manage the rescue of Credit Lyonnais with that of state-controlled insurer GAN, whose losses are expected to total 12 to 15 billion francs.
Newspaper reports suggested negotiations with Brussels could be acrimonious over what assets the Commission would demand the bank sell in exchange for approving fresh aid.
Most attention was focused on the fate of its 51 percent stake in Germany's BfG which analysts suggest could trigger a capital loss of some 4.4 billion francs if sold.
The government said on Friday it did not expect the bank to be ready for sale until the end of 1998 or the start of 1999.
